question: The father is the hostage. He is being held by the kidnapper, who is with him and has the daughter on the phone relaying the demand: 100 million yen, alone, by noon, no police. Because the father is himself the captive, he knows the money cannot save him—the kidnapper intends to kill the hostage regardless—and the only person who could actually raise and deliver the ransom is his daughter, who would have to bring it "alone." Delivering the money would put her directly in the killer's hands and endanger her life. Hearing the demand, the father therefore decides the ransom should not be paid: paying would not save him and would expose his daughter to the very danger he wants to spare her. Protecting his daughter, not the futile money, is why he refuses.

question: The father is himself the hostage. The kidnapper is with him and has the daughter on the smartphone: she begs for a life to be spared, while the kidnapper shouts the demand—100 million yen, alone, by noon tomorrow, no police. Because the father is the captive, he knows the money cannot save him: the kidnapper is with him and will kill the hostage regardless of payment. He also knows the only person who could raise and deliver the ransom is his daughter, and the kidnapper insists she bring it "alone," without police or anyone to protect her. Complying would therefore not rescue the father; it would only enrich a killer and force his daughter to walk unaccompanied into danger, since both father and daughter confirmed that her coming alone would put her at the kidnapper's mercy. That threat to his daughter—rather than any willingness or ability to pay—is what makes the father decide the ransom should not be paid. His refusal is meant to keep his daughter out of the trap the kidnapper has set.
